articles.exam: A2 Key · Reading Part 2 (true / false / doesn't say)
articles.headline: The Pope will have an operation
articles.standfirst: Pope Leo XIV says doctors found a small problem in his lung. People in Peru are sending him their best wishes.
body: Pope Leo XIV is the leader of the Catholic Church. On Sunday 11 October, he spoke to people at the Vatican. He told them that doctors found a small nodule in his lung. A nodule is a small lump.
The Pope said the doctors found it very early. They think it is best to take it out. So he is going to have an operation in the next few days.

Many people in Peru are thinking about him. The Pope lived and worked in Peru for many years, and he is planning a visit to the country. Peru's President, Keiko Fujimori, wrote a message on the social media site X. She wished him a fast recovery.
On Sunday, the President also went to a special Mass at Las Nazarenas Sanctuary in the centre of Lima. People there prayed for the Pope's health.

glossary.d: one of the two parts inside your chest that you use to breathe
a small, hard lump that grows inside the body
when a doctor cuts into a person's body to repair or take out something
the time when you get well again after you are ill

articles.headline: Back home in the forest: eight orangutans are free again
articles.standfirst: People saved the apes from big fires in Borneo. Now they are going back to the wild.
body: Orangutans are big orange apes. They live in the forests of Borneo and Sumatra, two islands in South-East Asia. They are in great danger. A hundred years ago there were more than 230,000 orangutans. Now there are only about 104,000.

This summer there were big fires in the forests of Borneo. There are fires every dry season, but this year they were much stronger because of El Niño, a change in the ocean that brings very hot, dry weather. In August and September, people in Indonesia rescued 46 orangutans from the fires.

Last Friday, eight of the animals went back to the wild: three mothers, their three daughters and two adult males. An animal rescue group took them to a reserve in the west of the island. The reserve has food and water, and it is connected to other forests, so the apes can move safely.

articles.headline: Loom and hand: the weavers of the Sacred Valley
articles.standfirst: An American woman who fell in love with Cusco as a teenager now helps 200 Quechua weavers sell their work around the world.
body: When Kennedy Leavens first visited Peru, she was only 17. She travelled from the United States with a group of students from her school, because their teacher's sister lived in Peru. At first, Kennedy felt ill because of the altitude, but soon she fell in love with the Sacred Valley of the Incas, near Cusco, and with the friendly people she met there.

She never forgot that trip. Today Cusco is her home, and she runs an organisation called Awamaki. The name comes from two Quechua words: awa, which means 'loom', and maki, which means 'hand'. Kennedy and the women she works with chose the name together.

Awamaki works with about 200 women from Quechua communities around Ollantaytambo. They use traditional techniques that their grandmothers also knew. Many of the women did not go to school, or only went for a few years, so the organisation helps them to weave to exact sizes and to keep the colours the same. It also teaches them about business and tourism.

The designs are created together with the weavers. Kennedy says the team does not copy fashion trends from other places. Their textiles are sold in a shop in Ollantaytambo and in shops in the United States, Japan, Australia, France and the United Kingdom. This means the women can earn money without leaving their communities or their traditions.
This year, Kennedy is part of 'More Peruvian Than Ever', a campaign that celebrates 15 years of the Peru country brand, Marca Perú.

glossary.d: how high a place is above the sea; at high altitude some people feel ill
a machine or frame used for making cloth from thread

a plan of activities to tell people about something

articles.headline: India's World Cup-winning cricket captain steps down
articles.standfirst: Harmanpreet Kaur made millions of Indians love women's cricket. Now a younger player will lead the team.
body: For almost ten years, Harmanpreet Kaur has been the captain of India's women's cricket team. Now she has decided to step down. Her long-time vice-captain, Smriti Mandhana, who is 30, will be the new captain of the team in every format of the game.

Harmanpreet, who is 37, became famous in 2017. In the semi-final of the Women's World Cup that year, she scored a century – 100 runs or more – against Australia. India lost the final to England, but millions of Indians began to follow women's cricket. Eight years later, in 2025, she led India to its first women's World Cup trophy. This year the team also won the Asia Cup and the Asian Games.

However, things changed after a disappointing T20 World Cup in England a few months ago. Harmanpreet was not batting well, and India's cricket board wanted a younger leader. According to reports, she hoped to stay captain in the longer forms of the game, but the board preferred Mandhana. Former players did not agree about the decision: some said it was time for a change, while others said her experience was too valuable to lose.
Harmanpreet shared an emotional message on Instagram. She said she had given the team everything and now wanted to play 'for the love of the game'. She plans to keep playing for India.

articles.headline: A legend in the hills: Roman fort may prove an old Welsh tale is true
articles.standfirst: For centuries a medieval story placed a Roman emperor's camp near a hill in Wales. Archaeologists may finally have found it.
articles.instructions: For each question, choose the paragraph (A–E). Each paragraph can be chosen once.
body: A. For centuries, people in Wales have told a story about Magnus Maximus, a Roman emperor who ruled Britain in the fourth century. In a collection of medieval Welsh tales known as the Mabinogion, he appears under his Welsh name, Macsen Wledig, and sets up his camp at Frenni Fawr, a 395-metre hill in Pembrokeshire. Until now, however, there was no archaeological evidence that the Romans had ever been there.

B. That may be about to change. Dr Mark Merrony, a specialist in Roman history at the University of Oxford, noticed the outline of a large shape in an overgrown field while studying satellite images. When he visited the site in 2024, about 3.5 kilometres south-west of the summit, he spotted a piece of Roman tile on the ground – the first of many.

C. This year, a team paid for partly by the university and partly through crowdfunding carried out the first of several planned excavations. Before the dig, Merrony's brother Nick joked that he should find a couple of coins to prove his theory. To everyone's amazement, Nick then came across two coins from the late fourth century – the period when Magnus Maximus was in power.

D. The fort measures 180 by 150 metres and sits on a slope with a wide view of the surrounding countryside. It has the typical Roman 'playing-card' shape with rounded corners and probably housed around 500 soldiers. The diggers have found pottery, large numbers of tiles, clay floors, an unusual iron writing tool and even the marks left by wagon wheels.

E. The discovery also changes what historians believed about the region. It had been assumed that the local Celtic tribe lived peacefully alongside the Romans, but a heavily defended fort suggests otherwise. Surveys of the ground show a central building facing east, which Merrony believes was the headquarters, next to what was probably the commander's house.

glossary.d: from the Middle Ages, about the years 500 to 1500

collecting small amounts of money from many people, usually on the internet

the main building from which an organisation or army is controlled

articles.headline: Three stripes against four: Adidas takes a fashion brand to court
articles.standfirst: The German sportswear giant says an Australian label's striped clothes are too similar to its famous design.
body: How many stripes does it take to start a legal battle? For the German sportswear company Adidas, the answer appears to be four. The company is taking White Fox, a fast-fashion brand based in Sydney, to the Federal Court of Australia, claiming that its four-striped clothes are "deceptively similar" to Adidas's famous three stripes.

Adidas has owned the three-stripe trademark in Australia since 1957, and it argues that the design has built up a valuable reputation. According to the company, White Fox has been selling sweatpants and shorts with four parallel stripes of equal width since at least March, and has refused repeated requests to stop. Adidas's lawyers told the court that White Fox intended to profit from the bigger brand's reputation.

Some of the evidence concerns advertising. Adidas says one online advert for White Fox socks showed a model wearing pink Adidas shoes, which could make shoppers think the two brands were connected. It also claims that, after the case began, the stripes on those shoes were digitally removed from the picture.

White Fox denies doing anything wrong. Its lawyers say they will point out that several other Australian labels sell clothes with similar decorative stripes. A trial lasting three to four days is expected early next year. If Adidas wins, it wants White Fox to hand over the profits from the clothes, plus interest and costs.

The German company has won a similar battle before: in 2013 it successfully sued another firm in Australia over shoes with four stripes. White Fox, meanwhile, has grown fast. Launched in 2013 by a couple from Sydney, it is popular with teenagers and young adults in Australia, the UK and the US, and its yearly sales have risen about four times since 2022.

articles.headline: Who will connect India? A very public fight over satellite internet
articles.standfirst: Elon Musk says powerful interests are keeping Starlink out of India. The government says everyone is being treated the same.
body: Satellite internet promises to reach places that cables and phone masts never will – and in a country as vast as India, that promise is worth fighting over. This week the fight became unusually public, as Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX owns the satellite internet service Starlink, accused powerful business interests of keeping his product out of the country.

Starlink, which delivers internet access from satellites in low Earth orbit, has been trying to enter India since 2021. It has already obtained key licences, but it still lacks the final security clearances and the allocation of radio spectrum it needs to start commercial services. Musk, pointing out that Starlink is licensed in more than 165 countries, first blamed unnamed wealthy business owners and then singled out Mukesh Ambani, Asia's richest man, whose Reliance group owns Jio, India's biggest mobile network. Musk went as far as asking whether Ambani was "the real boss of India".

India's government rejected the accusation. The Ministry of Communications said that Starlink, Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio's own satellite company were all at roughly the same stage of the approval process, each waiting for security checks and spectrum. It described claims of unfair treatment as baseless. Neither Ambani nor Reliance has responded.

What makes the quarrel peculiar is that the rivals are also partners. In March 2025, both Reliance Jio and its competitor Bharti Airtel signed agreements with SpaceX to distribute Starlink equipment in India, subject to government approval – even as each prepares a satellite service of its own. At a technology conference in Delhi, Jio's chairman, Akash Ambani, declined to comment on the row, saying only that the company wanted to concentrate on its customers.

Security lies behind much of the caution. In 2024, Indian authorities said they had found Starlink equipment during a drug-smuggling investigation in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and during an army operation in Manipur; Musk replied that the service had never been active in India. There are also questions about price: it is not yet clear whether rural families, the very people satellite internet is supposed to help, could afford it.
For now, millions of Indians in remote areas remain poorly connected, while some of the world's wealthiest people argue over who will connect them.

articles.headline: Slow, ancient and unwanted: Greenland argues over the fate of its sharks
articles.standfirst: Fishers say the sharks are costing them money. Scientists warn that one of the ocean's oldest creatures cannot survive a cull.
body: Few animals take life as slowly as the Greenland shark. It is the slowest shark in the world, yet it can grow to six or seven metres long and live for more than 400 years. It is also thought not to become an adult until the age of about 150. Now this remarkable creature has found itself at the centre of a bitter argument in the Arctic.

The problem lies in the cold waters off Greenland's west coast, where fishers catch halibut and cod – the same fish the sharks like to eat. Sharks that go after the catch often get tangled in fishing gear, cutting lines and costing fishers money. One young fisher from Ilulissat, Greenland's third-largest town, told the Guardian he had lost around 6,000 hooks this year alone.

Earlier this year, the local municipality of Avannaata approved a plan to cull 1,000 sharks, offering fishers 300 Danish krone for each one. Its mayor argued that the community had to protect fishers' incomes and the foods people had eaten for generations. The plan was eventually dropped after Greenland's government questioned whether it was legal, but the idea has not gone away.

Conservationists are alarmed. Because the species reproduces so slowly, it is still recovering from heavy fishing in the 19th and 20th centuries; in 1948 alone, 58,000 sharks were landed. One marine scientist described the Greenland shark as probably the ocean's most sensitive species when it comes to overfishing. A local conservation group adds that a cull would not even work: the sharks travel up to 2,000 kilometres a year, so any removed from one area would soon be replaced by others.

Others argue that the shark is being blamed for deeper problems. Fishing makes up about a quarter of Greenland's economy, and the industry faces too many boats, tight quotas, rising costs and few other jobs. The average size of halibut is shrinking, and fishers also complain about 'ghost lines' – lost or abandoned fishing gear left in the sea. Seen this way, the shark is less a cause of the crisis than a symptom of it.
